message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, but you can quickly check your upload/download speeds yourself.  
Below are a couple of easy options you can try on a Windows machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Quick web‑based test  
Open a browser and go to one of the popular speed‑test sites:

| Site | What it shows |
|------|---------------|
| [speedtest.net](https://www.speedtest.net) | Download, upload, ping |
| [fast.com](https://fast.com) | Download only (Netflix‑powered) |
| [speedof.me](https://speedof.me) | Download, upload, ping, jitter |

Just click “Go” (or “Start”) and let the test run. It will give you a clear read‑out of your current speeds.

---

## 2️⃣ Command‑line test with **speedtest‑cli**  
If you prefer a terminal/PowerShell approach, the `speedtest-cli` tool is handy.  
It’s a Python script that talks to Speedtest.net’s API.

### Install (if you don’t already have it)

```powershell
# If you have Python 3 installed:
python -m pip install speedtest-cli
```

### Run the test

```powershell
speedtest
```

You’ll see something like:

```
Testing from Your ISP (Your City)...
Retrieving speedtest.net configuration...
Testing download speed........................................
Testing upload speed..........................................
Download:  85.23 Mbit/s
Upload:    12.45 Mbit/s
Ping:      24.7 ms
```

---

## 3️⃣ DIY PowerShell download test  
If you don’t want to install anything, you can use PowerShell to download a known‑size file and measure the time.  
Here’s a quick one‑liner that downloads a 100 MB test file from Hetzner and reports how long it took:

```powershell
Measure-Command {
    $client = New-Object System.Net.WebClient
    $client.DownloadFile('https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin', "$env:TEMP\hetzner_test.bin")
}
```

The output will look like:

```
Days              : 0
Hours             : 0
Minutes           : 0
Seconds           : 12
Milliseconds      : 345
Ticks             : 123456789
TotalDays         : 0.000138
TotalHours        : 0.003312
TotalMinutes      : 0.19872
TotalSeconds      : 11.9232
TotalMilliseconds : 11923.2
```

From the `TotalSeconds` value you can calculate the speed:

```
Speed (Mbps) = (FileSizeInBits / TotalSeconds) / 1,000,000
```

For a 100 MB file (≈800 Mbit):

```
Speed ≈ 800 / 12 ≈ 66.7 Mbps
```

*(Replace `100MB.bin` with a different file size if you want a more precise measurement.)*

---

### Quick recap

| Method | Best for | How to run |
|--------|----------|------------|
| Browser test | Anyone | Visit speedtest.net or fast.com |
| `speedtest-cli` | Terminal lovers | `speedtest` after installing via pip |
| PowerShell download | No install needed | `Measure-Command { … }` |

Pick the one that feels most comfortable for you. If you run into any hiccups or need help interpreting the results, just let me know!
